<section class="page-intro"><p class="section-number">Note · Tools for thinking</p><h1>A useful local agent earns its keep</h1><div class="article-meta"><span class="status">Published</span><span>05 Sep 2026</span></div></section>
<article class="prose"><p>A small local model can produce an answer quickly. That does not yet tell me whether using it saved work.</p>

<p>I would judge a local agent by the useful result after verification.</p>

<h2>Give it a job with a finish line</h2>

<p>“Improve this repository” is difficult to assess. “Locate the configuration loader and identify the callers that depend on its defaults” has a clearer output.</p>

<p>A bounded task makes it easier to provide relevant context and check the answer. It also makes a failed attempt easier to discard.</p>

<h2>Compare the whole workflow</h2>

<p>For a repository question, I would compare two routes:</p>

<ul><li>Find and verify the answer with ordinary search and inspection.</li><li>Ask the local agent, then verify its answer against the same source.</li></ul>

<p>The comparison should include preparation, generation, review, corrections, and unsuccessful attempts. If setup is reused across many tasks, report it separately rather than hiding it.</p>

<p>A reduction in remote-model tokens can be useful. It is not the same measurement as reduced time or improved correctness.</p>

<h2>Keep the useful failure cases</h2>

<p>An agent that names a plausible but nonexistent function creates work. An agent that points to the correct file but misreads a condition still needs correction.</p>

<p>Those cases belong in the assessment alongside successful answers.</p>

<p>Local Agent Toolkit provides a bounded interface for this kind of work. Its existence does not establish a fixed saving across models or tasks.</p>

<p>The question I care about is practical: after checking the result, am I further ahead?</p>
</article>
